name: GHK-Cu
route: Injected under the skin (unapproved) or applied to skin in cosmetics
status: Not FDA-approved as a drug; injectable use is unapproved and its compounding status was under FDA review as of 2026
mechanism: Carries copper into cells and appears to switch on repair programs in skin cells, raising collagen and blood-vessel growth in lab and animal studies

article.summary: GHK-Cu is a natural copper-binding tripeptide used in skincare and sold as an unapproved injectable for skin, hair and healing. Human evidence for injection is essentially absent.
article.takeaway: GHK-Cu is a three-amino-acid peptide that occurs naturally in blood and grabs copper tightly. In lab and animal work it boosts collagen, wound repair and blood-vessel growth, and its levels fall with age.[^1] Human evidence is thin: one older trial found faster healing of diabetic foot ulcers with a GHK-Cu gel,[^2] and cosmetic studies are small. **No controlled human studies support injecting it**, and the FDA has flagged a possible immune-reaction risk with injectable products.[^3] Topical copper peptide skincare is a separate, lower-stakes question covered under [copper tripeptide-1](/peptides/copper-tripeptide-1).
glance: Not an approved drug; injectable compounding status under review as of 2026
Skin rejuvenation, wound healing, hair growth, general anti-aging
Skincare products; unapproved injections sold online or through some clinics
Mostly lab and animal studies; a few small human skin and wound trials
Safety and benefit of injections, long-term copper exposure, product quality

blocks.text: GHK (glycine-histidine-lysine) was identified in human plasma in the 1970s and is also found in saliva and urine. It binds copper with an affinity similar to albumin's copper-carrying site, forming GHK-Cu. Researchers have proposed that it is released from tissue proteins after injury and acts as a local repair signal.[^1]

items: **Skin matrix:** raises production of collagen, elastin and other support molecules by fibroblasts, while also adjusting the enzymes that break them down[^1]
**Repair cells:** attracts immune and blood-vessel cells to wounds in animal models[^1]
**Gene activity:** computer analyses of gene-expression databases suggest it nudges thousands of genes, a finding that has not been tested as a treatment[^1]

rows: Diabetic foot ulcers, randomized trial with GHK-Cu gel (1994)
Median ulcer closure 98.5% vs 60.8% with a placebo gel, plus fewer infections; the product never became an approved drug[^2]
Skin after CO2 laser resurfacing, 13 patients
No objective difference in redness or wrinkles; patients using GHK-Cu reported higher satisfaction[^4]
Lab and animal effects are consistent, but human evidence is sparse and often poorly characterized[^5]

blocks.text: Much of the enthusiastic literature comes from a small number of groups, including the peptide's discoverer, and many claims rest on cell or animal experiments. There are no published randomized trials of injected GHK-Cu for skin, hair, healing or aging in people.

items: **Injections:** the FDA notes limited human safety data and a risk that peptide aggregates in compounded injectables could trigger immune reactions[^3]
**Product quality:** online "research use only" vials have no FDA oversight for purity, dose, sterility or copper content
**Topical use:** skincare concentrations appear well tolerated, though irritation is possible

blocks.text: The long-term effects of repeatedly injecting a copper complex are unknown, and no studies have examined use during pregnancy or in people with a history of cancer.

GHK-Cu is not an FDA-approved drug for any use. In 2023 the FDA placed injectable GHK-Cu on its list of compounding substances that raise significant safety concerns. In April 2026 that listing was dropped after the nominations were withdrawn, but that did not make injectable GHK-Cu eligible for compounding.[^3] Non-injectable (topical) GHK-Cu remains under evaluation for compounding,[^6] and the FDA said it would ask its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee to review GHK-Cu before the end of February 2027.[^7]
Cosmetic copper peptide products are legal to sell as cosmetics as long as they make no drug claims.

GHK-Cu is a real, biologically interesting molecule with decades of lab research and modest support as a skincare ingredient. The leap to injecting it for anti-aging or healing is not backed by human trials, and gray-market products add quality risks. Anyone considering it should discuss it with a clinician who knows their medical history.

evidence.label: Low: lab and animal data, few small human studies
evidence.text: Laboratory and animal findings are plentiful,[^1] but human evidence is limited to one older wound trial and small cosmetic studies, and a 2026 review judged the clinical evidence sparse.[^2][^5] Injected use has no controlled human data.

faq.q: Is GHK-Cu the same as the copper peptide in my serum?
faq.a: Yes, chemically. On ingredient lists it appears as copper tripeptide-1. Applying it to skin is a different proposition from injecting it, with different risks and evidence.
Lab and animal studies suggest effects on hair follicles, and a few small human cosmetic studies exist,[^5] but there is no solid evidence that it treats hair loss.
It is not FDA-approved, and as of 2026 it is not an accepted substance for pharmacy compounding.[^3] Vials sold as research chemicals are not meant for human use.
